extracted.intended_audience: middle-level mathematics educators, teacher educators, and course developers (professional development designers)
extracted.subtask_description: Designing and delivering graduate-level or in-service professional development courses for middle-level (grades 5–8) mathematics teachers, emphasizing content knowledge, pedagogy, formative assessment, and classroom-applicable investigations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modeling ways educators might effectively share mathematical concepts
rubrics_metrics.description: Throughout our courses, we model ways that educators might effectively share mathematical concepts with their own students.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use investigations that can be adapted for middle level students; when adult learning materials go beyond middle-level scope (e.g., Eratosthenes’ circumference calculation involving geometry and trigonometry), demonstrate and discuss how to modify materials for middle level classrooms. Provide explicit examples and discuss classroom modifications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differentiated activities for heterogeneous classes
rubrics_metrics.description: Since many educators face heterogeneous middle level classes, we also provide differentiated activities and experiences to expand their understanding and to add relevant activities to their repertoire.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include scaffolded and extended versions of tasks, identify multiple entry points, and offer tasks that support varied readiness levels so teachers can adapt to mixed-ability classrooms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emphasis on formative assessment
rubrics_metrics.description: We emphasize formative assessment in our courses. At the beginning of each course, educators take a pre-assessment on course content and pedagogy, and take it again at the end. We also model formative assessment by using exit questions twice a day.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implement pre- and post-assessments (including validated instruments where possible), frequent exit questions (morning and afternoon), gather daily feedback on successes and needed changes, and use results to plan subsequent activities. Provide final feedback collection at course end. Use pre-post measures to evaluate impact (e.g., statistically significant gains).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of exit questions as quick formative checks
rubrics_metrics.description: We regularly incorporate exit questions (usually at the end of morning and afternoon sessions) to measure educator facility with major concepts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design succinct prompts that reveal conceptual understanding (examples provided: define 'proportional relationship'; risk comparison or design a graphical display). Revisit or extend topics based on exit question performance; use exit questions to guide next instruction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attention to mathematical language and graphic organizers
rubrics_metrics.description: Because students’ mathematical challenges often arise from difficulties with mathematical language, we give attention to this in our courses. We incorporate many graphic organizers, such as concept maps and cluster-word webs, to help teachers organize and communicate their ideas about course topics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Model and practice tools (concept maps, cluster-word webs, Frayer Model) and discuss how to use them with middle level students. Use organizers to analyze vocabulary (essential/inessential characteristics, examples/non-examples).

rubrics_metrics.name: Frayer Model for term analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: We have used the Frayer Model to help analyze and describe important terminology under consideration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Have educators create Frayer models for terms (e.g., 'proportional') covering essential/inessential characteristics and examples/non-examples. Discuss classroom applications and share successful teacher uses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Review and analysis of student work to inform instruction
rubrics_metrics.description: In most of our courses, we devote time to review student work, analyze student errors and misconceptions, and discuss how this might inform instruction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide authentic student work samples, guide analysis of misconceptions and reasoning, and use findings to suggest instructional moves and follow-up questions. Encourage educators to bring/analyze their own students' work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Final project: analyze pre-test results and plan instruction
rubrics_metrics.description: Educators in all of our courses complete a final project in which they explore some aspect of their own students’ work. (Proportional Reasoning final project specifications are given.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example final-project specs (Proportional Reasoning): (1) Create and administer a pre-test to assess students' proportional reasoning; analyze results and summarize findings; discuss implications for instruction. (2) Select one item from the pre-test and student work pieces (both correct and incorrect) and discuss numerical relationships, context, and follow-up questions. (3) Choose three students (different readiness levels) and create a display of their work; discuss levels of reasoning and instructional responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Course delivery: multiple formats and recommendation for intensive summer institute
rubrics_metrics.description: We have presented this course several times as a summer institute, in-service sessions, an independent study course, and as an evening course during the academic year; the intensive summer institute approach seems to be the most successful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider offering both on-site intensive formats and blended/distance options; weigh advantages for participant engagement and follow-up. Provide access to syllabus and daily agendas for different delivery modes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of investigations, technology, and manipulatives
rubrics_metrics.description: Courses use activities such as 'I Spy' photo analyses (using Geometer’s Sketchpad), spinner probability applets, handmade clinometers, building figures with cubes, and the 'Penny Experiment' to investigate proportional ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Incorporate hands-on, visual, and technological tools to support conceptual understanding (Sketchpad, applets, clinometers, manipulatives). Scaffold investigations for varying levels and encourage data collection, measurement, simulation, and analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emphasis on proportional reasoning across strands
rubrics_metrics.description: Proportional reasoning is the most significant theme throughout middle level mathematics. This course emphasizes proportional relationships and contrasts them to non-proportional relationships and connects to NCTM strands.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design activities that apply proportional reasoning in number, geometry, algebra, measurement, functions, and data; include real-world contexts and cross-strand connections to deepen understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Follow-up session for project presentations and continued engagement
rubrics_metrics.description: The follow-up session, held in the fall, is devoted to educators’ presentations of research projects; discussions are typically lively and engaging.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan follow-up meetings (face-to-face or online) for participants to present projects, reflect on classroom implementation, and sustain professional learning communities. Consider asynchronous online options (discussion boards, virtual worlds) if scheduling is difficult.

rubrics_metrics.name: Daily assignments and final problem set
rubrics_metrics.description: Educators receive assignments each day of the course, including readings (e.g., Lamon’s Teaching Fractions and Ratios for Understanding) and problem solving in proportional reasoning. In addition to action research projects, educators complete a final problem set.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide nightly work that reinforces daily topics, readings from relevant journals/books, and cumulative problem sets that require application and reflection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incorporate an Equity Framework explicitly
rubrics_metrics.description: We have incorporated features of the Equity Framework in our course design and made them explicit to educators.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use equity-focused design principles: attend to heterogeneous classrooms, ensure access and high-level tasks for all learners, and make equity considerations explicit in planning and instruction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance intellectual rigor for adults with classroom applicability
rubrics_metrics.description: We faced the issue of maintaining intellectual rigor of adult learning while still offering direct classroom applications and addressed it by focusing on important mathematical ideas and building skills in meaningful contexts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select tasks and content that are deep and challenging for adult learners but include explicit discussion and modification strategies to make activities appropriate for middle level students.

rubrics_metrics.name: Engage groups in complex problem solving and delegate authority
rubrics_metrics.description: We have engaged groups in complex problem solving that requires collaboration, and we delegated authority for learning, requiring independent research and application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design tasks requiring collaborative problem solving, assign roles, promote learner-led inquiry, and require participants to conduct independent investigations and classroom applications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use research on student learning and misconceptions to guide content
rubrics_metrics.description: We have focused on research on how students learn the relevant mathematics content, and where they have misconceptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Base curriculum choices on established research; present common student misconceptions and strategies to address them; model diagnosis and instructional responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematical habits of mind as explicit course goal
rubrics_metrics.description: The courses aim to help participants become productive mathematical thinkers with a toolbox of skills and knowledge to experiment, conjecture, reason, and solve problems — 'mathematical habits of mind' such as flexibility of thinking, use of indirect arguments, making connections, understanding why algorithms work, ease of calculation and estimation, persistence, and metacognition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make habits of mind explicit learning objectives; design tasks and reflections that cultivate flexibility, argumentation, connections between concepts, and metacognitive reflection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Habits-of-mind problems: selection criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Problems need not be connected to the mathematics being studied but should be solvable. Ideal problems involve experimentation or consideration of special cases and require careful reasoning and creativity to solve.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose problems that invite multiple solution strategies, encourage exploration of special cases, support conjecturing/proof, and are accessible yet rich enough to foster deep reasoning (examples: grid-path problems).

rubrics_metrics.name: Active learning and group-centered instructional style
rubrics_metrics.description: Our approach emphasizes active learning: participants are given a problem to solve, often working in groups; solutions are presented by participants followed by mini-lectures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structure sessions around problem solving, small-group work, participant presentations, and targeted instructor-led debriefs. Support peer instruction and multiple solution method sharing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Instructional support structure (team teaching, advisors, study groups)
rubrics_metrics.description: We try to have five instructors in the room at one time (two university mathematicians, two graduate students, and one master teacher). Each night participants have 3–4 hours of homework with instructional team members joining study groups. Tuesday mornings begin with small group meetings with Staff Advisors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide a multi-person instructional team for just-in-time support, organize nightly study groups with facilitator support, and schedule regular small-group advisor meetings for participant reflection and problem discussion.

rubrics_metrics.name: End-of-course assignment with 'super six' and reflection
rubrics_metrics.description: End-of-Course Assignment: comprehensive take-home final including (1) new mathematics problems covering course content, (2) a 'super six' (or seven) — polished solutions to problems participants completed during the course, and (3) a reflection component in which participants reflect on their growth in mathematical understanding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Require polished work and metacognitive reflection to reinforce learning and promote retention. Allow several weeks to complete and emphasize quality and explanation in submissions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Class size and workload expectations
rubrics_metrics.description: Class size is 32–35 and we try to have five instructors in the room. Each night participants have three to four hours of homework.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan staffing to support large cohorts, set realistic nightly workload (3–4 hours) and communicate expectations clearly. Provide scaffolding and limited, timely assistance so participants struggle productively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adjective-noun framework for understanding numbers
rubrics_metrics.description: Numbers are viewed as adjectives that modify nouns (e.g., '5' modifies 'ones' or 'fourths'), which helps with place value, measurement, and fractions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teach and model the adjective-noun language for numbers to reduce common errors (e.g., adding denominators incorrectly) and to support classroom explanations of place value and fraction operations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Course content sequencing and daily themes (MSL)
rubrics_metrics.description: MSL Day-by-day themes: Day 1: Algebra vs. Arithmetic, From Hieroglyphics to Place Value, Understanding Addition; Day 2: subtraction and signed numbers; Day 3: multiplication, area, Pythagorean Theorem; Day 4: division and fractions; Day 5: fractions to decimal representations and rational/irrational comparisons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sequence topics to build from fundamental arithmetic concepts to connections with algebra and geometry; include historical/contextual elements and multiple representations to deepen conceptual understanding.
